metadata.title: Does the relationship between competitiveness and student achievement vary based on the culture of competitiveness? Evidence from PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata with a two-stage stratified sampling design (schools sampled first, then students within schools). It reports that it applied both student-level and school-level weights provided by PISA to account for unequal selection probabilities and nonresponse. The analysis is conducted in Mplus 8.10 using ten plausible values for mathematics, combined with multiple imputation for missing data, and then estimated in a three-level hierarchical linear modeling framework (students nested in schools nested in countries). The manuscript does not name the exact PISA weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT), so readers should use the standard PISA 2018 student and school weights from the dataset documentation when replicating.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 mathematics achievement (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) as the dependent variable and included only countries/economies for which mathematics plausible values and the competitiveness climate items (ST205) and the World Values Survey-based culture of competitiveness were available. The final analytic sample contains 57 countries/economies for the country-level culture variables and 57 country observations, while student and school observations are 436,343 and 16,312 respectively. The manuscript explicitly excludes 22 of the 79 PISA 2018 participating countries/economies (Austria, Belgium, Brunei Darussalam, Canada, Costa Rica, Denmark, Iceland, Italy, Ireland, Israel, Kosovo, Luxembourg, Macao, Malta, Montenegro, Panama, Portugal, Qatar, Russia (Moscow City, Moscow Region, Tatarstan), Saudi Arabia, Vietnam, United Arab Emirates). Missing data were handled via multilevel maximum-likelihood multiple imputation in Mplus, generating ten imputation datasets that were combined with the ten mathematics plausible values for analysis.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level HLM (Model 4): Student competitiveness B=8.916 (p<0.001, 95% CI [8.034, 9.798]); Competitiveness climate B=14.194 (p<0.01, 95% CI [5.813, 22.575]); Cross-level interaction Student Competitiveness×Culture B=1.056 (p<0.05, 95% CI [0.334, 1.777]). ICCs: school-level 18.6% and country-level 18.6% in Model 4.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) the study leveraged Student competitiveness, Competitiveness climate, and Culture of competitiveness (plus key student/school/country controls) to model mathematics achievement, finding that higher student competitiveness and a more competitive school climate were associated with higher mathematics achievement and that the culture of competitiveness strengthened the student-competitiveness/achievement relationship. This indicates that education systems may benefit from aligning classroom/school competitive practices with broader socio-cultural expectations, while also monitoring that competitiveness effects are not uniform across countries.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 mathematics achievement for 15-year-olds using ten plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) combined with multilevel multiple imputation for missing data, and estimates three-level hierarchical linear models (students nested in schools nested in countries). The analytic sample includes 436,343 students from 57 PISA countries/economies for which both competitiveness climate items and a country-level culture-of-competitiveness index (from the World Values Survey) were available. In the final cross-level interaction model, student competitiveness showed a positive association with mathematics achievement (B=8.916, p<0.001), and competitiveness climate at school level was also positively related (B=14.194, p<0.01). The culture of competitiveness significantly moderated the student-competitiveness effect (interaction B=1.056, p<0.05), while the school-competitiveness climate moderation was not significant. Because the design is cross-sectional and the analysis is correlational (not causal), the results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper uses advanced multilevel modeling and plausible values, it does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive algorithms (no supervised ML learners such as Random Forest/XGBoost/SVM are reported). Therefore, ml_techniques is intentionally left empty and the research design is classified as exploratory rather than predictive/causal.
